stances.claim: To understand the changes made in the Feb 3 2015 SC en banc resolution (released Feb 11), we must first review the original July 1 2014 decision -- annually Congress enacts the GAA with itemized expenditures, and the Constitution prohibits transferring appropriation from one PAP to another except under the limited 'power of augmentation' exception for five specifically-named officers

The Court held four DAP acts unconstitutional: (1) transfers of savings prior to fiscal year end (savings not generated unless PAP completed/discontinued/abandoned); (2) cross-border transfers between branches; (3) transfer to non-GAA PAP; (4) UF transfer without national treasurer certification that revenue exceeded targets

Under the doctrine of operative fact, these unconstitutional acts remain valid and public officials who committed them in good faith are not culpable -- but the doctrine 'cannot apply to the authors, proponents and implement[e]rs of the DAP' unless tribunals find good faith

The new resolution deleted 'proponents and implement[e]rs' but retained 'authors' -- this deletion is fair because proponents and implementers were innocent participants; even Sen. Jinggoy Estrada who 'exposed' DAP did not know funds came from augmentations

The Court also clarified that 'authors' enjoy the presumptions of innocence, good faith, and regularity in the performance of official duties -- eroded only if and when after proper charges are filed and due process observed by DOJ/OOO/trial courts

Plainly, the government won because the Court partially granted its motion for reconsideration by limiting personal liability only to 'authors' and only after other tribunals find evidence of bad faith and culpability -- otherwise stated, the DAP decision cannot, by itself, be a source of liability

The constitutional exception is quite difficult to comprehend -- even the keenest legal minds can misconstrue it; the SC itself on March 5, 2013 asked for cross-border transfer of P100M from DOJ to judiciary for Malabon Hall of Justice (withdrawn Dec 23, 2013 after DAP petitions filed); hence it is fair and reasonable that the doctrine of operative fact should validate past acts

Far from condemning DAP, the Court said it is a policy instrument the Executive may utilize to spur economic growth and development; unlike PDAF, the Court did not find public money flowing to private pockets, pseudo foundations, or fake NGOs -- at bottom, it is reason, logic, and fairness that really won

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban dissects the Supreme Court's February 3, 2015 en banc resolution modifying its July 1, 2014 decision that had declared four specific acts under the Disbursement Acceleration Program unconstitutional. The press statement was issued on February 3 but the resolution itself was released to the public only on February 11. To understand the changes, CJ first reviews the original decision: annually, Congress enacts the General Appropriations Act containing an itemized list of expenditures for the three branches and the independent agencies like the Comelec; under the Constitution, money allotted for one program, activity, or project cannot be spent for another, much less for one not included at all; even Congress cannot 'authorize the transfer of appropriation' from one item to another. The Constitution allows one exception: the President, the Senate President, the Speaker of the House, the Chief Justice, and the heads of the Constitutional Commissions may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the GAA for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations -- the 'power of augmentation.' The Court held four DAP acts unconstitutional or illegal because they failed to follow this strict exception: (1) transfers of savings 'prior to the end of the fiscal year' (savings are not generated unless the PAP has been legally completed, discontinued, or abandoned); (2) cross-border transfers at any time from one branch to another (e.g., executive to legislative); (3) transfer to a PAP not in the GAA; (4) transfer of unprogrammed funds without a certification from the national treasurer that revenue collections exceeded the total revenue targets. The Court further ruled that, under the doctrine of operative fact, these acts though unconstitutional remain valid and public officials who committed them in good faith are not culpable -- but the doctrine 'cannot apply to the authors, proponents and implement[e]rs of the DAP, unless there are concrete findings of good faith in their favor by the proper tribunals.' In its new resolution, the Court deleted 'proponents and implement[e]rs' but retained 'authors.' Proponents refer to lawmakers, governors, mayors who requested funding; implementers are the executive officers who built or undertook the PAPs. This deletion is fair because the proponents and implementers were innocent participants -- even Sen. Jinggoy Estrada, who 'exposed' the DAP, did not know that the funds came from augmentations. The Court also clarified that the 'authors' enjoy the presumptions of innocence, good faith, and regularity in the performance of official duties -- eroded only if and when, after proper charges are filed and due process observed in specific cases, other tribunals (like the DOJ, the OOO, and trial courts) find enough evidence showing their bad faith and culpability. Further, in relation to Item 3, the Court said that 'as long as there is an item in the GAA for which Congress has set aside a specific amount of public fund, savings may be transferred thereto for augmentation purposes.' And in relation to Item 4, unprogrammed funds may be used on a quarterly basis 'upon proof that the total revenues exceed the target.' Who won? Plainly, the government won because the Court partially granted its motion for reconsideration by limiting personal liability only to the 'authors' of the DAP, and only after other tribunals find evidence of bad faith and culpability -- otherwise stated, the DAP decision cannot, by itself, be a source of liability. Clearly, the constitutional exception is quite difficult to comprehend. In fact, on March 5, 2013, the Court itself asked for the cross-border transfer of P100 million from the DOJ's budget to the judiciary for the construction of the Malabon Hall of Justice -- a request that was withdrawn on December 23, 2013, after the petitions questioning the constitutionality of the DAP were filed. This shows that even the keenest legal minds can misconstrue the exception. Hence, it is fair and reasonable that the doctrine of operative fact should validate past acts and that everyone, including the 'authors,' should be given the presumptions of innocence, good faith, and regularity in the performance of official duties. Far from condemning it, the DAP, said the Court, 'is a policy instrument that the Executive, by its own prerogative, may utilize to spur economic growth and development.' Moreover, unlike in the case involving the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF), the Court did not find any public money malevolently flowing into private pockets, or to pseudo foundations, or to fake nongovernment organizations. At bottom, CJ thinks it is reason, logic, and fairness that really won.
